webTitle: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate | Editorial

fields.headline: The Guardian view on AI money in US politics: not the way to hold an urgent democratic debate
fields.trailText: Editorial: Amid public concern over the impact of new technology, Silicon Valley’s use of its wealth to influence specific election races is an unwelcome development
fields.bodyText: As the huge societal ramifications of artificial intelligence have become clear, some of the tech industry’s most senior figures have taken to writing thinkpieces on what comes next. The latest to do so is Mark Zuckerberg, who this week published 6,500 words making the case for a laissez-faire approach to AI development. Worrying too much about regulation, Meta’s CEO unsurprisingly opines, could lead to the United States falling behind in the race to own the future. Mr Zuckerberg’s plea for maximum autonomy is, of course, self-serving. Much of his essay – which airily envisions “invention superpowers” for every entrepreneur and “an abundance of jobs in the future” – reads like unadulterated tech-utopianism. But the lobbying at least has the merit of being out there in the open. As midterm elections loom in the US, darker arts are also being used to counter popular concern about what AI will mean for a host of topics, from the labour market to child safety, the environment and cybersecurity. Replicating a strategy deployed by cryptocurrency backers in the 2024 election cycle, Silicon Valley is pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Super Pacs – groups unaffiliated to political parties or campaigns – to ensure that voices sympathetic to its deregulatory AI agenda get elected. OpenAI’s co-founder and president, Greg Brockman, and Palantir’s co-founder, Jo Lonsdale, have given large sums to Leading the Future, an organisation dedicated to “identifying, maintaining, and growing pro-AI candidates”. Vast amounts are being spent to try to tilt the balance in individual contests, sometimes through disingenuous means. Earlier this summer, Leading the Future spent $6m on ads attacking Alex Bores, a New York state assemblyman and pioneer of AI regulation at state level. Rather than focus on his AI campaigning, the ads attacked Mr Bores’s progressive credentials, alleging that he had carried out tech work in the past for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which he denies. Running for Congress in a Democratic stronghold, he lost a tight primary race after battling what was in essence a smear campaign. Countervailing forces are emerging. Guardrails Alliance, a union-backed Super Pac, is attempting to combat Leading the Future’s influence, while a bipartisan groundswell of opposition to datacentres is generating serious electoral clout. But as tech companies and their billionaire owners seek to shape and above all limit the scope of AI regulation, their influence is distorting debate in a political culture where the power of money already holds far too much sway. In his essay, Mr Zuckerberg urges that AI’s democratising potential be protected from those who believe “a small set of experts … should decide what is best for humanity”. He appears to miss the irony that an unelected tech oligarchy, to which he belongs, is already performing that function by default. Its pressure has been instrumental in persuading Donald Trump to cancel the signing of an executive order which would have given the government the right to review new AI models. Its wealth is now being used to attack and undermine dissenting voices in the public square. If a democratic debate about the benefits and dangers of AI is to take place, such presumption must be fiercely resisted in the US and elsewhere. The semi-covert manipulation of political discussion is no way to map out an inclusive future in challenging times.

webTitle: Republicans name candidate to replace Chuck Edwards after sexual harassment investigation

fields.headline: Republicans name candidate to replace Chuck Edwards after sexual harassment investigation
fields.trailText: Jennifer Balkcom to face Democrat Jamie Ager in race to represent North Carolina’s 11th congressional district
fields.bodyText: North Carolina Republicans on Monday chose the state lawmaker Jennifer Balkcom to replace Chuck Edwards, the incumbent congressman who earlier this month dropped his re-election bid after a US House investigation determined his conduct towards young female staffers probably amounted to sexual harassment. Balkcom will face off against the Democratic nominee, Jamie Ager, in the November midterm elections to represent the 11th congressional district in western North Carolina. Though Donald Trump won the district by 10 percentage points two years ago, Democrats believe Ager may have a shot at winning amid the president’s low approval ratings and frustration over the pace of recovery from Hurricane Helene, which devastated the region in 2024. “I’m blessed to receive the Republican nomination for the 11th Congressional District. Western North Carolina is where I was born, raised, and chose to raise my own family,” Ager said in a statement following her nomination. “Rest assured, I will work every single day between now and Election Day to earn the votes of our friends and neighbors. Our region is incredibly strong and resilient, and I plan to be the fighter everyone who calls Western North Carolina home deserves.” Edwards was first elected in 2022 after defeating the scandal-plagued congressman Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary. Last week, the US House ethics committee found he “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” towards two female employees in his Washington DC office. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior probably violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances, and the ethics committee recommended he be censured. Even before Edwards dropped out, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the House Democratic campaign arm, had added his district to its list of targets to regain the majority in the House of Representatives in November’s midterms. No House Democrat has won election to the region since 2010, and the race between Ager and Balkcom is likely to see concerted spending from both parties and outside groups. Edwards had won the Republican nomination for his district in last March’s primary, and the North Carolina Republican party had convened in Asheville a meeting of officials from the region to select a replacement. Zach Almond, the state party’s executive director, said Balkcom beat five other candidates on the first round of balloting.

webTitle: Doctors and lawmakers condemn Trump order calling for sweeping changes to childhood vaccines – as it happened

fields.headline: Doctors and lawmakers condemn Trump order calling for sweeping changes to childhood vaccines – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: That concludes our coverage of the second Trump administration for today. Here are the latest developments: President Donald Trump departed on a secret military flight from Turkey last month when the White House said he was flying aboard ⁠Air Force One, an extraordinary move prompted by an Iranian assassination threat, the Washington Post reported Monday. Donald Trump signed an executive order that will involve splitting up the highly effective measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three single shots. The president also announced an overhaul to the childhood immunization schedule, scrapping recommendations for the hepatitis b, Covid-19 and influenza vaccines. He also suggested that the number of inoculations are linked to the rate of autism in the US, despite no proven link between the two. Medical experts have blasted the changes, calling it “problematic and deeply concerning.” Todd Blanche has been sworn as US attorney general, cementing Trump’s installation of his former personal attorney in charge of the Department of Justice. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was confirmed in his new position during a ceremony at the White House on Monday. Trump has named White House staff secretary Will Scharf to become White House counsel and assistant to the president, replacing David Warrington, who is taking a job in the private sector. In taking up that role, Scharf will become the White House’s top lawyer after overseeing the administrative work of the Oval Office in his current position. Lawyers for David Hearn, the Olympian who was arrested for alleged property destruction of the reflecting pool before his charges were dropped, said that the Trump administration is “continuing to attack an innocent man”. Former Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall said on CNN that he will sue to force the Trump administration to restore his security clearance. Kendall’s clearance was revoked Friday after the administration claimed he had disclosed sensitive information about the Qatari-gifted jet now serving as Air Force One. Kendall has denied disclosing classified information. “As my mother taught me years ago, you stand up to bullies,” said Kendall. According to The Washington Post, an Iranian assassination threat against President Donald Trump prompted an operation in July, in which he had to secretly fly from Turkey on an alternate military aircraft while the White House said he was aboard Air Force One. The operation took place in Ankara, where the president had been for a NATO summit with world leaders. Trump boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras, and then he was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight, a US official told the Post. An official also confirmed the operation to the New York Times. Trump’s actual location was concealed from journalists and some White House staff members. A US official told the outlet that a credible threat to Trump involving Iran set the “deception operation” in motion. The administration had previously claimed that Trump left Turkey on 8 July on the former Air Force One. The president had also announced on Truth Social that he would use the “former Air Force One” rather than the plane that flew him there, a new Boeing 747-8 gifted by Qatar. Medical experts and lawmakers are blasting Donald Trump’s executive order calling for sweeping changes to childhood vaccine recommendations. The order calls for fewer childhood vaccines and would require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be broken into three separate shots. It would also recommend that all shots be given at separate medical visits, promoting the president’s long-held but baseless theory that the shots should be spaced out. Jan Carney, president of the American College of Physicians, called the changes “problematic and deeply concerning.” “This executive order is part of a troubling pattern by the administration to attempt to unilaterally change vaccine guidance, particularly for children, rather than relying on the transparent, scientific review that has guided the US childhood vaccine schedule for decades,” Carney said in a statement. “If implemented, the changes could increase costs to patients and families, including additional copays while also placing a greater burden on families needing to schedule multiple appointments for a multiple-dose MMR vaccine.” Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said current vaccine recommendations are “based on decades of research and systematic tracking of real-world experiences.” “Pediatricians recommend children receive certain vaccines at specific ages based on when children’s immune systems will respond best and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases,” Racine said. “Sometimes this means children will receive a single shot that protects against multiple diseases, or they may receive multiple vaccines at one visit.” Democratic representative Frank Pallone, meanwhile, said in a statement that Trump’s executive order cuts out “the expertise of independent scientists altogether.” “Parents deserve accurate, trusted medical guidance, not a White House-curated list designed to rubberstamp Secretary Kennedy’s radical anti-vaccine agenda,” Pallone said. “I urge the Administration to reverse course before this executive order doubles down on the damage done to public trust and the health of our nation’s children.” Democratic senator Patty Murray urged parents to “listen to your doctor NOT Trump or RFK Jr.” “IGNORE Trump’s Executive Order,” Murray said. “There is NO link between vaccines and autism. In the middle of actual public health crises America deserves leaders informed by actual science. FIRE RFK Jr.” Politico is reporting that members of the Trump administration asked Ohio Republicans not to wage a public pressure campaign against the embattled representative Max Miller despite allegations of domestic abuse against him. The move comes as Miller has decided to stay in the race despite mounting calls for his resignation, refusing to step aside as the Republican nominee for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District ahead of Monday afternoon’s deadline. Trump administration officials argued that messaging would get complicated if the same leaders who called for Miller’s resignation would later have to defend him in the general election. “They basically told us to back off,” an Ohio Republican involved in the conversations told Politico, “and let the voters decide.” Donald Trump’s administration is facing questions over whether it is using Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to “surveil political opponents” after an investigative agent was apparently stationed outside Democratic representative Ilhan Omar’s monthly town hall meeting in Richfield, Minnesota. After the incident, Omar demanded the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) clarify whether Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents have been used to monitor “any other activity” involving “local, state, or federal officials” in the state. In a letter to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), an arm of ICE, the congresswoman said an agent claiming to be conducting an undercover drug operation was parked outside the community center where she was holding an event last Thursday, without prior coordination with local law enforcement. According to Omar, who represents Minnesota’s fifth congressional district, a Richfield police officer noticed the agent sitting in a Ford Explorer and “became suspicious of the way she was monitoring the building”. Read the full story here: Republican senator Bill Cassidy, a trained physician, called Trump’s latest executive order spacing out childhood vaccines “wrong.” “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong,” he said in a post on social media. “The President does not have the expertise to make these changes.” “Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism,” Cassidy added. “Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe.” “Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” he wrote on Monday. A judge has temporarily blocked New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax, which would place a surcharge on second homes in the city, the Wall Street Journal reports. The emergency pause comes after a group of homeowners filed a lawsuit against Mamdani and the city’s finance director over the tax last week. They allege the city wrongly identified their homes as potentially subject to the surcharge despite the properties serving as their primary residences. “The city has arbitrarily and capriciously foisted onto New York City residents the burden of proving they are not subject to the surcharge,” reads the complaint filed on Friday. Amid the judge’s order on Monday, the city is barred from issuing any additional notices. Mamdani’s critics accuse the democratic socialist mayor of targeting the wealthy, while others have welcomed the tax, seeing it as a helpful way to raise revenue from affluent property owners in a city grappling with a high cost of living. Also asking Max Miller to step aside are members of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, one of whom called the allegations against the congressmember “horrific” and “credible.” “The horrific allegations levied against Max Miller, who has a lengthy record of alleged domestic violence, are credible and cannot be ignored,” said DCCC spokesperson Riya Vashi. “Rather than step aside, Miller has chosen to cling to power and put his family and his constituents through a public spectacle of his own making,” Vashi added. “Let’s be clear: this is the same playbook Max Miller has run before — deny, deflect, and drag his accusers through the mud.” The Trump administration has extended for 90 days ⁠a waiver allowing foreign-flagged ships carrying oil and gas to travel between US ports, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a post on social media. The waiver extension, which will take effect on 17 August, applies to the Jones Act, a law passed in 1920 that requires shipping between ports in the US to be conducted under US ships. Rogers said the extension was granted to “ensure our military and key industries maintain uninterrupted access to critical resources”. “Data shows the waiver has driven a significant increase in domestic deliveries of essential products such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel,” Rogers wrote. New limits were imposed after shipbuilders and members in Congress argued the policy was undermining the domestic maritime ⁠industry. Now, the waiver will only apply to cargo that are sources of energy and commodities related to agriculture, per the AP. The waiver comes as the strait of Hormuz, a primary waterway for shipping oil and natural gas, remains effectively closed because of the war. Ironworker Brian Poindexter, a Democrat challenging the embattled congressman Max Miller in Ohio, said that his opponent “should be in prison, not in Congress” if the allegations of domestic abuse are true. “It’s unfortunate that Miller has chosen to keep putting his ex-wife and her family through this nightmare in the public spotlight,” Poindexter said in a statement. “But let me be perfectly clear. I got into this campaign to fight for my neighbors and for working people across this district,” he added. “That continues to be my north star. Our campaign’s doors are wide open to anyone - Democrat, Republican, or anything in between - who believes their representative should serve with honor and work for Ohioans, not for special interests and not for themselves. In November, we will win this race, and the people of the 7th District will finally have a representative who fights for them.” Speaking to reporters earlier, Donald Trump said that the US retains the full capability to escalate actions against Iran if it chooses to do so. “We have certainly that ability if we want to do that,” Trump said. “You’ll find out.” Echoing remarks he wrote in a Truth Social post, Trump said Iran should pay for “the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period” instead of the US paying for the damage caused by the bombardment in Iran over the past five months. “They ask for money for the damage that we’ve done. I said: ‘that’s a good idea. Well, we’re going to ask for money for the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period’,” he said. “If there’s damages to be paid, I think Iran should pay those damages.” Donald Trump signed an executive order today that will involve splitting up the highly effective measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three single shots. The president also announced an overhaul to the childhood immunization schedule, scrapping recommendations for the hepatitis b, Covid-19 and influenza vaccines. He also suggested that the number of inoculations are linked to the rate of autism in the US, despite no proven link between the two. Todd Blanche was officially sworn in as the new attorney general. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was narrowly confirmed in the role by the Senate. Every Democrat rejected Blanche’s nomination. Lawyers for David Hearn, the Olympian who was arrested for alleged property destruction of the reflecting pool before his charges were dropped, said that the Trump administration is “continuing to attack an innocent man”. This comes after Donald Trump said that Hearn was still guilty on Truth Social this weekend, despite the justice department dismissing all charges against him, and citing the “botched” renovation of the pool as the reason for the peeling lining. Trump also said today that he is “demanding compensation from Iran” in future talks. This comes after Tehran tied compensation for the damage caused by the war launched by the US and Israel at the end of February to the reopening of the strategic strait of Hormuz. Trump said the matter of compensation “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings”, but Tehran has been demanding war damages from Washington since the early weeks of the war. Later he said that Iran should be responsible for “the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza”. The Trump administration has repeatedly pointed to Europe as a model – arguing that EU countries do not require childhood vaccinations. In reality, 12 EU nations mandate certain vaccines for children. France, Germany, Italy, Hungary, Croatia, Bulgaria, Czechia, Latvia, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia all require the measles vaccination for infants, for example. As my colleague Melody Schreiber notes, while Trump’s latest order requires clinicians to offer three separate shots to protect against measles, mumps and rubella, there are actually no separately licensed vaccines for the diseases, and the licensing process takes years. A reminder that the changes recommended to the childhood vaccine schedule were first suggested by the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP) earlier this year. However, they were blocked by a federal judge. We can expect that these latest attempts overhaul the immunization schedule will be met by further legal challenges. In the Oval Office, Donald Trump has signed an executive order – that we flagged earlier – which would split up the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. “You should have five separate visits for vaccines rather than giving them all in the same day,” the president said. He added that his administration would no longer recommend hepatitis b, Covid-19 and influenza shots for children. “Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today. In those times, people were much healthy, and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. So there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was,” Trump said, despite the fact that there is no proven link between inoculations and an increased risk of autism. Earlier, we reported that Trump is “demanding compensation from Iran”, tied compensation for the damage caused by the war launched by the US and Israel. In a follow-up post on Truth Social, the president said that Tehran should be responsible for “the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza”. In a closed-press ceremony, Todd Blanche was officially sworn in as the new attorney general. In a video posted to social media, press secretary Karoline Leavitt filmed Blanche taking the oath of office while Donald Trump stood beside him in the Oval Office. Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since April. The Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation in the role, with the Republican-led upper chamber voting 50-49 in the early hours of Saturday morning. Every Democrat rejected his nomination. Donald Trump is set to sign an executive order today that will involve splitting up the highly effective measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three single shots. Last year, the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP), which health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr overhauled and replaced with several vaccine-skeptics, voted to change US vaccine policy and recommend single vaccines to protect against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox, instead of a single shot that can protect against all four diseases. Kirk Milhoan, the ACIP chair, telegraphed earlier this year that he expects the US childhood vaccine schedule to undergo changes. ACIP may “not necessarily” change the recommendations for all vaccines to become optional, but the committee is “reevaluating all of the vaccine products including risks and benefits”, Milhoan told the New York Times in January. Many public health experts have warned that splitting up shots could increase the likelihood of missed visits and reduced immunization. 2026 has already seen the highest number of measles cases throughout the US in 35 years, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Meanwhile, in Charleston, South Carolina, defense secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled that the area’s main airbase has now been renamed in honor of the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham. “It now falls to us to continue Senator Graham’s work, of building up our military, the hard work of defending this nation,” Hegseth said, while unveiling Joint Base Lindsey Graham. The late lawmaker served for three decades in the US military, retiring with the rank of colonel. Todd Blanche has arrived at the White House for his swearing-in ceremony. The event is currently closed to the press, but we’ll let you know if anything changes. Joe Gruters, the Republican National Committee (RNC) chair, avoided calling on Max Miller – the embattled Ohio congressman facing a wave of domestic abuse allegations and pressure to resign – to end his re-election bid. “I always tell people that there’s not many things worse than divorce,” Gruters said in an interview with NewsNation. “Nobody’s a winner.” A reminder that Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, is the daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno, also a Republican. Many of the accusations against Miller came out through the custody battle court filings for their two-year-old daughter. Gruters added that the RNC “will support our nominees”. Despite the many calls for Miller to abandon his campaign for his seat that is a GOP stronghold, the incumbent did not withdraw by the deadline needed for Ohio Republicans to select a replacement nominee. “We need to make sure we hold the majorities. Max, I’m sure, is on that side,” Gruters said. “Everybody has to prove that they’re capable of winning, and then we’re gonna look at our resources and make the decisions. I can’t tell you right now … I hope that he can. We hope we can hold that seat in Ohio. It’s an important seat, but we’re going to be watching that race very carefully.” Ahead of Todd Blanche’s formal swearing-in today, the NAACP has said that the new attorney general earned his job “by defending Donald Trump”. “His record is clear: he’s attacked voting rights, abandoned civil rights enforcement, targeted Trump’s political enemies, and he’s looked the other way when civil rights are threatened,” said NAACP president Derrick Johnson. “The Department of Justice should be the guardian of justice, not a shield for political corruption. Once again, this Senate has let us down.” A reminder that Blanche secured his confirmation last week, after Republican Senator Bill Cassidy cast a deciding vote and saved his nomination. Donald Trump has said he is “demanding compensation from Iran” in future talks after Tehran tied compensation for the damage caused by the war launched by the US and Israel at the end of February to the reopening of the strategic strait of Hormuz. In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the matter of compensation “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings”, but Tehran has been demanding war damages from Washington since the early weeks of the war. In April, Tehran demanded compensation after US-Israeli attacks wrought an estimated $270bn worth of destruction, and said the issue had been discussed in talks with Washington in Pakistan. That figure was later revised up to $400bn, but the two sides later settled on a $300bn investment fund and other measures to support Iran’s economic recovery. Trump has insisted that American taxpayer dollars will not fund that project, instead it will be funded by private investment, including from the Gulf states. Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi toughened Tehran’s demands over the weekend, declaring that the reopening of the strait of Hormuz is conditional on the US agreeing to a long list of demands, including paying Tehran financial compensation. Here’s Trump’s full Truth Social post: I see that Representatives of the Islamic Republic of Iran are asking for compensation for the damage done to them during the last five month Military Conflict (started because, THEY WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON), even though it was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings! But it is an interesting idea because now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by General Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat. Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protestors that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months. I have instructed my representatives to put this firmly into any, and all, future negotiations. Donald Trump has named White House staff secretary Will Scharf to become White House counsel and assistant to the president, replacing David Warrington, who is taking a job in the private sector. In taking up that role, Scharf will become the White House’s top lawyer after overseeing the administrative work of the Oval Office in his current position. Trump also appointed him chair of the National Capital Planning Commission last year, where he helped secure approval for the $400m for the White House ballroom project. He served as the general counsel of Trump’s 2024 campaign and also previously represented Trump in a number of criminal and civil legal cases in between his two terms in office, including the presidential immunity case at the supreme court. Trump made the announcement on Truth Social last night, saying Scharf would start on 1 September. “I know Will well! He previously represented me in numerous cases, including at the Supreme Court, during the Biden Administration’s corrupt and illegal campaign of Weaponization,” the president wrote. He added: “Will is Tough, Strong, and Smart! He also loves our Country, and respects the Law. Will Scharf will do a great job as White House Counsel!” Lawyers for David Hearn, the Olympian who was arrested for alleged property destruction of the reflecting pool before his charges were dropped, said that the Trump administration is “continuing to attack an innocent man”. This comes after Donald Trump said that Hearn was still guilty on Truth Social this weekend, despite the justice department dismissing all charges against him, and citing the “botched” renovation of the pool as the reason for the peeling lining. Hearn’s lawyers also said they are still “reviewing all legal remedies, including for this continued harassment”. A Kurdish man who was force-fed over the course of eight months while on hunger strike in US immigration detention has spoken out about it for the first time, describing how much the process harmed him physically and psychologically. Gabar Choli, a film-maker and activist now living in Canada after being deported, described how he endured the coercive treatment – a practice widely considered torture by international human rights groups – often twice a day after being detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) when his asylum application was denied. “It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said in an exclusive interview with the Guardian. “It came to a point that I decided to write my body an apology letter.” ICE officials force-fed Choli at the Port Isabel federal detention center in Los Fresnos, south Texas, from late May 2025 until he was deported in January of this year, a Guardian investigation found. Choli had resorted to a hunger strike to protest against conditions at the facility and to push for a resolution to his immigration case. He described how a team of detention center guards would physically restrain him while ICE medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his esophagus and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach. An investigation by the Guardian last week found that the second Trump administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures. Wisconsin is not the only state with high stakes primary races on 11 August. We’ll also be bringing you the latest on a number of pivotal contests. In Minnesota, the closely watched and crowded Democratic primary for US Senate seems to be a competition between lieutenant governor Peggy Flanagan and congresswoman Angie Craig. Meanwhile in the state’s gubernatorial race – the Republican primary is shaping up to be a three-way competition between Trump ally and fervent election denier Mike Lindell, businessman Kendall Qualls and Minnesota House speaker Lisa Demuth. On the Democratic side, four-term US senator Amy Klobuchar is the frontrunner hoping to succeed outgoing governor Tim Walz. There are also primaries in Alabama, Vermont and Connecticut on Tuesday. And we’ll be covering the special Republican primary to replace the late Senator Lindsey Graham on the general election ballot. As Francesca Hong surged ahead in the final weeks of the chaotic Democratic primary to be Wisconsin’s next governor, the democratic socialist has become the internet’s main character. Donald Trump has mocked her old tweets, while major figures in her own party publicly questioned her ability to win a general election. The man she is vying to succeed even launched a late blitz in support of one of her rivals. But on the ground in Wisconsin, the enthusiasm for her shines through. In hundreds of events across Wisconsin – from karaoke nights to ramen pop-ups – Hong, 37, built a grassroots army that pushed her to the verge of clinching the Democratic nomination for governor in a marquee battleground state. After the progressive Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for US Senate in next-door Michigan last week, scrutiny of Hong intensified. In Wisconsin, Democrats face another test of whether voters in a swing state will side with leftwing candidates in primaries – and what that could mean for the party’s chances in a typically close general election in November. Hong – a chef and former restaurant owner, a single mom and a state lawmaker from Madison – is running on a progressive platform that includes universal childcare and fully funding the state’s public schools. She is also calling for a moratorium on datacenters, a centerpiece that differentiates her from the other Democratic candidates. “I got into this race because I know that we can win and that Wisconsinites are going to fight for one another and fight to be a part of the change,” she told the Guardian, “because they’re tired of people making decisions that don’t improve lives and they’re tired of the status quo.” Four candidates are vying for the open governor’s seat on Tuesday, with most polls showing Hong in the lead. Kelda Roys, a state senator, and Joel Brennan, a former head of the state administration department, are still in the race. David Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, exited the race and then re-entered it – receiving the endorsement of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers. A memo from the Crowley campaign on 5 August suggested polling may be off, pointing to Michigan polls showing El-Sayed with a much broader lead than he actually achieved. Evers recently claimed Hong’s campaign was “in a tough place”, because she had to spend time dealing with “what’s on the Twitter”. Reach Rachel’s full dispatch from Milwaukee, Wisconsin here: Donald Trump appeared to acknowledge that “some contractor error” done by rushing the reflecting pool renovation job for a 4 July opening. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that the mishandled work “was a very small area” of the pool of “and was relatively inconsequential”. However, Trump also continued to insist that former Olympian David Hearn was guilty of vandalism, despite the justice department dismissing the property destruction charges against him for having touched a chunk of the reflecting pool’s newly peeled lining. In a Truth Social post, the president cited a line from a court filing that notes that a national parks employee saw Hearn “ripping and tugging at the Pool’s somewhat delicate coating”. However, Jeanine Pirro – the US attorney for the District of Columbia – dropped the charges against Hearn last week. In a 20-page court filing, Pirro’s office wrote that the damage to the concrete-bottomed tourist attraction was the result of a “botched” renovation – “not vandalism”. Trump has since decried Pirro’s decision, claiming his longtime ally and former Fox News host “folded like an umbrella”. “She made a terrible mistake. I don’t understand why she did such a stupid thing,” the president told NBC News last week. On Tuesday, Republican voters in South Carolina will have the opportunity to re-select their GOP nominee for the Senate race this November. This comes after the death of long-serving Senator Lindsey Graham last month. Graham had won the Republican nomination for the Senate seat he had held for 23 years. His sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to finish the final months of his term and is running to take his place as the GOP nominee. She’s also received Trump’s endorsement. Tuesday’s special primary is already a crowded race, and Darline Graham will have to face off against nine other candidates, including congressmen Russell Fry and Ralph Norman, former South Carolina governor Mark Sanford and businessman Mark Lynch. webTitle: Judge temporarily blocks Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax on second homes

fields.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax on second homes
fields.trailText: New York mayor’s office plans to appeal ruling, which comes after homeowners sued over property surcharges last week
fields.bodyText: A judge has temporarily blocked Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax, which would place a surcharge on second homes in New York City, dealing a blow to the progressive New York City mayor after homeowners sued over the policy. The tax would apply to people who own, but do not reside full-time in, any house worth more than $5m, or a condominium or cooperative unit worth at least $1m. The temporary, emergency pause comes after a group of homeowners filed a lawsuit against the mayor and the city’s finance director over the tax last week. They allege the city wrongly identified their homes as potentially subject to the surcharge despite the properties serving as their primary residences. “The city has arbitrarily and capriciously foisted onto New York City residents the burden of proving they are not subject to the surcharge,” reads the complaint filed on Friday. The temporary pause was issued by a state judge on Monday, the Wall Street Journal reported, and means the city is barred from issuing any additional letters notifying homeowners of their potential tax liability and taking down a public list of properties. The city published a tax roll of about 960,000 owners who could be subject to the tax. It also sent notices to 17,000 addresses. Announcing the tax in April, Mamdani and Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said it was expected to generate $500m in annual revenue. Mamdani’s critics accuse the democratic socialist mayor of targeting the wealthy, while others have welcomed the tax, seeing it as a helpful way to raise revenue from affluent property owners in a city grappling with a high cost of living. The proposed tax on multimillion-dollar second homes, known as pied-à-terres, comes as Democrats are trying to address voter concerns about affordability ahead of this year’s midterm elections. Critics, including prominent business leaders, Republicans and some moderate Democrats, have warned that slapping new taxes on rich people who maintain apartments and townhouses in New York, but don’t consider it their primary home, will lead the very wealthy to abandon the city. In a statement to the Guardian, Matt Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for Mamdani, criticized the ruling and said the mayor’s office planned to appeal. “We disagree with today’s ruling, but we are confident in both the pied-à-terre surcharge and the City’s ability to implement it fairly and effectively,” Rauschenbach said. “This surcharge asks those who own second homes valued at $5 million or more to contribute their fair share to the city they benefit from. The Law Department will appeal the ruling immediately which will stay the order, and the City will continue with the pied-a-terre’s implementation.” Associated Press contributed reporting
